source.title: Unlearning What Matters: Token-Level Attribution for Precise Language Model Unlearning

record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates unlearning outcomes and retained capability for existing sequence-level methods, but does not test recovery attacks. Its results bear on the unlearning and retention parts of version A using benchmark accuracy measures.
record.gate_note: The paper reports no fine-tuning, activation-ablation, quantization, or prompting recovery tests. Its statement that adversarial probing and relearning attacks are future work is not a result. Rows below cover the reported sequence-level WMDP baselines; the TokenUnlearn variants are the paper's new method compared with baselines and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: This paper proposes a method, TokenUnlearn. It uses the original's WMDP benchmark and RMU method, together with GA, WGA and NPO, as sequence-level baselines. It reports only forget and utility scores (Table 1 for TOFU, Table 2 for WMDP/MMLU/MT-Bench) to compare those baselines with its own token-level variants. It runs no fine-tuning, activation-ablation, quantization or prompting recovery attack. The Limitations section says relearning and adversarial-probing attacks were 'not evaluated', and the paper makes no robustness claim. So it bears neither on A, which hinges on whether attacks recover the knowledge, nor on B-F.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that token-level variants of GA, WGA, NPO and RMU (hard selection and soft weighting) consistently beat their sequence-level counterparts on TOFU and WMDP across Phi-1.5 (TOFU only), Llama-2-7B and Qwen-3-8B. They report up to 32.6% better forgetting and up to 19.0% better utility. Table 2 has a few exceptions to 'consistently': for example, S-GA on Llama-2-7B Bio scores 43.3 against 42.2 for GA. They acknowledge that residual traces may persist and that adversarial-probing and relearning attacks were not evaluated.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes token-attribution-based hard selection and soft weighting, extending GA, WGA, NPO, and RMU; it does not reproduce a recovery attack or the cited original unlearning studies' recovery tests.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that selection ratio and entropy-signal weighting change TOFU outcomes; its stated default selection ratio is r = 0.2 and α = 0.7.
record.problems: No recovery attacks are evaluated, and the WMDP table reports no chance-level comparison. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the tabulated outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 TOFU results and Table 2 TokenUnlearn hard-selection and soft-weighting results were left out. Table 1 is flattened in the supplied text, making method-to-value assignment unclear; the new-method comparison results were also excluded under the row rule.

untested.parts: All. The WMDP/MMLU/MT-Bench numbers are baselines for the authors' own method, and no attack tests whether the knowledge can be recovered.
All; there are no relearning experiments.
All; there is no activation ablation or internal analysis of the unlearned models.
All; there are no rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context probes.
All. TokenUnlearn is neither claimed nor tested to resist attacks, and the authors say residual traces may persist.

record.verdict_notes:
Changes from the earlier verdict:
(1) The two grouped row_fixes items (comma-separated lists of 16 rows each), which the merge rejected, are now 32 items, one per row. Every row keeps the same judgment: versions ["none"], state cannot_determine. Each problem now names that row's subject, method, measure and values.
(2) A's untested entry now reads 'All' instead of only the attack part. The earlier verdict judged that the baseline numbers don't bear on A, so listing only the attack part as untested contradicted it.
(3) authors_conclusion adds that Table 2 has a few exceptions to 'consistently'.
Everything else is kept: relation uses_without_test, tranche T4 (it uses the original's WMDP benchmark and RMU method as tools), no labels, no fits_no_version, no missing.

Checks against the text: Table 2 is flattened in the text file. The record's assignment of values to methods follows the column order and fits the later T-/S- blocks. Cyber values for the baselines are 25.5-33.6, mostly near the 25% chance level; Bio values are 34.7-49.3, well above it. Only Bio and Cyber are reported, not Chem.

Paper inconsistencies: it says all three datasets use multiple-choice accuracy, but MT-Bench values are on the 10-point judge scale. The ablation text says Llama-2-7B, but the Figure 2 caption says Qwen3-8B.

A reader could take the re-run RMU baselines (e.g. Llama-2-7B Bio at 36.3, MMLU 57.9 to 50.3) as falling short of A's 'near chance with retained ability'. These are baselines for a competing method, though, with hyperparameters tuned on TOFU, so no verdict is drawn from them.

The text contains no instructions aimed at the reader.

versions.untested_parts: Whether simple attacks recover knowledge; whether the reported post-unlearning performance is near chance. The paper reports no recovery attack results.

rows.subject: Llama-2-7B
rows.note: Before-unlearning accuracy is the reference. The paper does not state a chance level.
rows.check: Sequence-level GA baseline, Llama-2-7B chat, WMDP-Bio, 64.1 -> 42.2 (Table 2). This is a baseline in the authors' comparison with TokenUnlearn, with no recovery attack, so it cannot show A's effect. Values read correctly. For context, 4-choice chance is 25%, so 42.2 stays well above chance.
